macro.topic: The Tera Portföy fund crisis and the state of money-market funds (PPF)

views.view: He argues money-market funds are entirely different from equity funds and should be considered risk-free; that the DSTKF shares pledged as collateral to the TP2 fund were returned to Tera, and that by regulation this must have been paid for with a liquid asset such as cash or bonds, meaning PPF investors will get their money back with interest.
views.quote: "There can't be a problem with your PPFs. These aren't risky asset groups at all... But all the collateral that carried risk has already been returned to Tera. So TP2 no longer holds any DSTKF share collateral... Everything else is either liquid or a valuable asset. It gets sold, your money gets paid. It's that simple."

views.view: He says the claim that '$17 billion evaporated' from the funds isn't real, that this figure was calculated from stocks inflated through manipulation, that fund managers don't actually have that much money either, and that what's really needed is a detailed analysis of the shares the funds hold.
views.quote: "Because as I understand it, the $17 billion isn't real anyway. It's a made-up figure calculated from stocks that were plainly inflated through manipulation. And no, the company's managers and owners don't have that much money either... What needs to be done here is a detailed analysis of the shares the funds hold."

views.view: He says he feels for a woman who lost all her savings in the funds, but argues the real problem stems from basic financial-literacy failures: concentration risk, keeping short-term cash like house money in risky assets, blindly trusting a banker's advice, and having no cash cushion.
views.quote: "Before putting all the blame on someone else, she should have taken precautions herself... Putting all her savings (eggs) in one basket... Putting short-term cash needs into risky assets. She'd paid a deposit for a house, planned to sell by end of September, but took no precautions... Not keeping a cash cushion."

macro.topic: The Fed's rate hike and the bond market's reaction

views.view: He explains that the Fed hiked rates by the expected 25bp to 3.75-4.0%, yet the 10-year yield still fell from 5.02% to 4.94% — driven by relief after the Saudi oil-pipeline strike, bond-market relief that inflation is being fought, the Fed's strong-growth framing, and the Bank of England also slowing its QT pace — which is why the Nasdaq and S&P 500 rallied despite the hike.
views.quote: "This week the NASDAQ was up by around 0.7% and the S&P 500 was roughly flat. However, if you look at the movement after the rate hike was announced... NASDAQ was up 1.7% and S&P 500 was up 1.1%... the 10-year bond yield actually went down a lot. It went down from around 5.02% to around 4.94%."

views.view: She notes that the US Treasury's long-bond buyback operation achieved only $2.4 billion against a targeted $4 billion, falling short of secondary-market liquidity support expectations, and that upward pressure on long-term yields persists.
views.quote: "Against the market's expectation of a $4 billion buyback, the Treasury completed only $2.4 billion in the auction... Following the results, upward pressure on long-term US Treasury yields was observed to persist."

views.view: She reports that a critical summit will be held at JPMorgan's headquarters where US Treasury Secretary Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng will discuss topics of global market importance such as trade tariffs, AI and rare earth elements.

persons.name: Bora Özkent
persons.digest:
Bora Özkent thinks the claim that '$17 billion evaporated' from the **Tera** funds isn't real; he argues the figure was calculated from stocks inflated through manipulation, and that the shares held by the funds need detailed analysis. He finds it illogical to argue that **Şişecam**'s poor performance pushed people toward the Tera funds, and says the company risking its capital with a share buyback could amount to 'suicide' in tough economic conditions.

In the video he published, he explains that you can't get rich from the stock market, describing how he made huge gains on **Tesla** and **Marathon Digital** in 2019-2022 but gave back most of them after Fed Chair Powell's Jackson Hole speech; he says what really matters is a business that generates steady cash flow, illustrating that the AI-powered portfolio platform he built now serves his members and speeds up his own analysis, and that starting with $100,000 at a 10% annual return plus an extra $10,000 invested monthly could reach $7.86 million in 20 years.

items.title: You Can't Get Rich From the Stock Market!
items.summary: His main thesis is that you can't get rich from the stock market, and what really matters is a business that generates steady cash flow. He describes making huge gains between 2019-2022 by buying **Tesla** at $13-14 as it rose to $420, and earning $100,000 overnight from **Marathon Digital**, but then giving back most of those gains after Fed Chair Powell said at Jackson Hole that they would raise rates to fight inflation. During that period he neglected his real income source (speaking engagements, his club), whereas with strong cash flow he wouldn't have panic-sold and wouldn't have taken those losses. He illustrates that starting with $100,000 and earning 10% a year could reach $673,000 in 20 years, and with an extra $10,000 invested monthly that figure could rise to $7.86 million. After that 2022 lesson, he says he built an AI-powered portfolio platform using AI, with a School membership model where members can track their portfolios and get analysis on the US stock market, which gives him steady cash flow and now lets him see downturns as opportunities rather than threats. He also stresses that Warren Buffett got rich from his own insurance business, not the stock market, and that the market is a mechanism that transfers money from the impatient to the patient.

assets.note: A past anecdote about buying Tesla at $13-14 between 2019-2022 as it quickly rose to $420, then giving back most of the gains after the Fed's announcement.

He attributes this drop to oil spiking above $100 after a pipeline strike on Saudi Arabia and then easing back via a ship-to-ship transfer, to the Fed's strong growth framing (the 2026 GDP forecast was revised up to 2.3%), and to the Bank of England holding rates steady while slowing its QT pace.

items.title: Fed hiked...but stocks are up..?
items.summary: His main thesis is that although the Fed hiked rates by the expected 25bp to 3.75-4.0%, the stock market still rallied. The NASDAQ was up 0.7% and the S&P 500 roughly flat for the week, but on the Thursday the hike was announced, the NASDAQ rose 1.7% and the S&P 500 1.1%; on Friday they added another 0.4% and 0.2% respectively. He notes this isn't textbook-expected, since a rate hike should normally raise the discount rate on companies' future cash flows and lower valuations. He lists three reasons: (1) the 10-year yield fell from 5.02% to 4.94% despite the hike, driven by oil spiking above $100 after a pipeline strike on Saudi Arabia and then Saudi Arabia bringing it back below $100 via a ship-to-ship transfer, plus bond-market relief that the Fed is fighting inflation. (2) The Fed's statement emphasized economic growth; the 2026 GDP forecast was revised up to 2.3% and the 2027 forecast to 2.4%. (3) The Bank of England also held rates at 3.75% and slowed its QT pace from £70 billion to £46 billion, easing pressure on global bond yields.

assets.note: It rose 0.7% for the week despite the hike, adding 1.7% on Thursday and 0.4% on Friday.
It closed roughly flat for the week but rose 1.1% on Thursday and 0.2% on Friday after the rate decision.

persons.digest: Ahmet Sunelcan notes that money at Turkish brokerages can't be considered fully safe, since a broker who wants to could commit fraud. For those with accounts at the US broker IBKR LLC, he explains that shares and cash are kept separate from the broker's own money, and that in the event of broker failure, SIPC covers up to $500,000 per account while Lloyd's excess policy — with a $900,000 cash sub-limit — raises total protection to as much as $30 million, though this coverage doesn't extend to market losses and all customers share a common $150 million pool; still, he sees value in not keeping everything on a single platform.

persons.name: cevikfinance
persons.digest: cevikfinance says he feels for a woman who lost all her savings in the **Tera** funds, but argues that mistakes such as concentration risk, keeping short-term cash like house money in risky assets, blindly trusting a banker, and having no cash cushion made the crisis worse, and that the real deficiency is financial literacy; on this he also criticizes Mahfi Eğilmez's article on regulatory responsibility, saying 'even the people you call experts turned out to be fraudsters'. He thinks **Meta**, with its new AI assistant **Muse**, has an opportunity to build an 'agent layer' on top of its ad and commerce ecosystem that could bring commission and payment revenue, and says his $1,000 **META** target still stands. He views Trump's 'AI Force' initiative as good news for AI stocks and says the **SMH** semiconductor index chart points to higher levels. He shares the Kobeissi Letter's analysis describing Europe as having become the 'sick man' due to the pandemic, the Ukraine war, falling behind in AI, US tariffs and the energy crisis from the Iran War.
